utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 23rd of September, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Scott and his team, and to all the people helping us out. I'll first give the floor to the registrar. He has an IC number for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The OTP has submitted its objections to documents tendered by 1D through Puljic, Borislav. This document shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00849. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Praljak will have the floor, he's ready, and I think he has 50 minutes left. Good afternoon again. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we tried to shed some light on this problem of the provision of electricity and transformers. I will be asking you some more questions about electricity and transformers in order to make this quite clear in terms of some basic concepts about the provision and distribution and generation of electricity. Could you please tell me, do you know that two large transformer stations, facilities in Cule, and switching stations in Cule to the north of Mostar. What was the name?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rastane.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Rastane, that at any rate in the Serb shelling in 1992 they were almost completely destroyed, both the switching facility and the transformer facilities.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, do you know that in Rudnik, a neighbourhood in Mostar on the western bank of the Neretva River, this provides electricity to a large section of the town, do you know that this transformer was also destroyed in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that transformers that are of a greater power must be out in the open because of cooling issues?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that for cooling purposes the transformer has something that is known as transformer oil?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Witness, how vulnerable is a transformer if a shell impacts nearby and then there are fragments? What if it goes through the sheeting or the isolated cables or if it hits the area where there's transformer oil and so on?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although a transformer appears to be a solid chunk of metal, it is very vulnerable in fact, a vulnerable piece of equipment, because it contains coils that must transfer the high-voltage electricity, the coolant in the form of oil, and a number of elements switching to -- connecting elements and other equipment that protects the transformer against sudden discharges such as those caused by lightning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So if any part thereof is damaged, we can consider this transformer to be out of order and out of use?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Now, we have to run some very thorough tests in order to determine the scope of the damage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If we're talking about damaged transformers, such as the one at Cule, we will not be bothering the Trial Chamber with the power, things like that, we don't want it to get too complicated. Could you please tell us how long does it take and what kind of blueprints and other documents have to be in place, how much time, how much money, is needed in order to install a transformer back in place and who should you apply to do that, who should do that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the Cule substation or transformer station which is close to Mostar, then we can say that it was one of the most complex transformer substations in the former Yugoslavia. It is -- it covers a large area and it is full of all kinds of electrical equipment, all kinds of transformers of various sizes, switching facilities, measuring equipment, optical cables, electronic equipment, and other things like fuses and so on. In order to build such a substation, you have to invest a large amount of money, tens of millions of euros, that would be the order of magnitude. And I think that Cule cost around 20 million euro, that's off the cuff, I seem to recall this figure. The reason why I know that is because the -- in order to fix, to repair, such a substation, you first need to do some thorough tests. You have to do the programme and also the project, how to do it, what needs to be done, and in what order. As far as the Cule substation is concerned, I know that because I was interested in this, that it took eight years to reconstruct the substation and that it cost approximately 10 million euro to do it. That's the information that I have at my disposal now, because we're not talking about a single transformer, it's a series of transformers of differing sizes used for various voltages in the transformation process.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But let's take just one transformer. Who manufactures it? Where do you order it? And if you have the money, if you have the -- all the blueprints and the project documents you go to Siemens and how long does it take for them to deliver it?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, transformer equipment is manufactured by a number of producers, but the most complex transformers for high-voltage systems have to be ordered especially and they're usually ordered abroad. So smaller transformers are manufactured as standard equipment. So you can get it sooner, but the larger the transformer -- it's a special-order equipment. It has to be constructed in a special way and then there is a longer delivery time. As far as I know, this transformer, the most complex one, the largest one, first of all let me say that those transformers in the former Yugoslavia were manufactured in several places, in Serbia, in Sarajevo, in Energoinvest, and they're still being manufactured in Zagreb in Rade Koncar, their production plant, but the most complex ones are brought abroad, usually from Germany, from Siemens. The delivery time for such transformers is more than two years. So it takes you some time to define what you need and then to negotiate. And once the contract is signed, you need to wait two years for the delivery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to take four documents to put them on the table and then we'll look at the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before you get those papers, could you please tell me if we're talking about smaller transformers, to 10 to 0.4 kilovolts, then the electricity is distributed to households and elsewhere. In Mostar how was this done? Was it done via underground cables or overhead cables?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we call the distribution grid. When the last transformation is done down to the 0.4 voltage, that would be 220 volts. This is usually done by cables in towns, but if you are not in a town, in other areas, it is usually done by aerial cables that are put on poles, wooden poles or concrete poles. This was sometimes also -- this is sometimes done by wire also. But in town it's usually done in urban areas, this is usually done via underground cables. You have to bear in mind that this is more expensive so you can't always do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first image. So this has nothing to do with what we would have drawn as engineers. This is something that is done for the laypersons, to be able to see how gradually the voltage is reduced, we can see here from 220 to 110 kilovolts, then larger numbers of transformers are switched on so that we can go down to what we need. My question to you is: For a town such as Mostar, which has its population and also various businesses, to be supplied with electricity, is there a whole network of transformers of various sizes and so on?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you picture this in a proper way. Usually there are substations, transformer stations in the outskirts of the towns, and they transform the voltage from 2010 and 110 kilovolts to lower voltages. Why are they located on the outskirts of the towns? Because electricity needs to be brought there by high-tension transmission lines, and those lines cannot be put around houses and inhabited areas. So you need to have corridors which are relatively unpopulated. And we're talking about high voltage which could lead to unwanted consequences. So electricity at a lower voltage, usually 35 kilovolts, is brought into the town and then you have the distribution grid where the voltage is 35 kilovolts, and then it is again transformed at the end-user point to lower voltages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will deal with just two more things. First, if an electricity power system is kept at the limit of its potential because there is not enough electricity and somebody switches on another transformer, is it possible for the grid to simply black out or parts of it to go down?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is highly possible because every substation, every piece of electrical equipment, has fuses in place that make it impossible to -- make it possible to limit the consumption to a certain level, that's a fuse cut-out. If it goes above this limit, then the fuses go out. If the fuses -- if proper fuses are not installed, then this brings into danger this piece of equipment, it is no longer protected by the fuses. That is why every time consumers tap into the lines in an unauthorised manner, and sometimes when they even cut themselves off from the grid, this can cause problems on a wider scale, in a wider area, and sometimes even complete black-out. This is why power systems are always linked up to cover the broadest possible area, and this is why the whole of Europe, the whole grid in Europe, is linked up. There are other reasons too, synchronisation to ensure the quality of the grid. This is also another important reason why the grid is fully linked. And the third important reason is to be able to exchange power because you always have moments where you have a surplus or a shortage of power, and then you can exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The last question related to electricity. Let us assume that somewhere on the transmission line leading to Stolac or somewhere else, one or two transmission pylons were torn down because of the shelling, for instance. Can you explain to the Judges and everyone else in the courtroom, what does it take to repair it. Who can do it? What transportation do you use to get there, mules or vehicles, how difficult is it to splice together the lines. How difficult is this in terms of technology and in terms of expense?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if something like that occurs, if a transmission line pylon gets damaged, which means that the transmission line is cut, and often it is only one line that is down, it is necessary to get there to the scene, those high-tension lines are usually in rugged terrain and they are accessible only on foot. And you have to carry all the equipment, all the supplies, either using beasts of burden or just carrying there yourself. It is always necessary to have experts with you, to have all the supplies and all the testing and measuring equipment, and to be able to reach the site. If this site is inaccessible, if mines are laid in that area - and that was often the case - then you first have to secure the area so that people could move around there, check for mines, demine the area, and then move on and fix it. Usually local companies have the capability to repair the lower-tension transmission lines. As for the high-tension power lines, they're unable to repair them. For example, if a pylon is damaged, it needs to be procured from the supplier, you don't have these in reserves, you have to purchase it, install it, and for this you need time and money and also the technical staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, could you please - and this is the usual practice in this Tribunal - place a date -- today's date and your initials on this sketch that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us give an IC number. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the diagram shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00850. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you look at the second sketch now, please. Again, I did the best that I could in the technical options that I had. I sketched in Mostar and those towns that I was able to number which were part of the regular PTT Mostar network. These cities, when phone calls were made from them, the communications first went to Mostar and then further out. So could you please explain to us how this functioned and then if we need to add anything we will do that.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar, as one of the transit switchboards or centres, of which there are four in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is linked with other transit exchanges and then the main exchanges are connected to that. In this case, these are Livno and Trebinje, and those main exchanges are followed by some node or end-user exchanges. All of those exchanges are directly connected to Mostar, and this is done by air. It doesn't mean that each location has a separate device. You can dial Mostar-Trebinje and then link Bileca with Mostar via Trebinje. In principle, the connections are overhead ones, aerial ones. So if Mostar falls, all of them fall as well; that is the idea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you please initial this sketch and give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second sketch shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00851. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's look at the next sketch. Yesterday, we had a little more complicated sketch yesterday. We see how Mostar was linked with Sarajevo by coaxial cable, and as far as I know Sarajevo was connected with Belgrade and Zagreb also by coaxial cable, and then Mostar via those relays as we saw yesterday was linked with Split, Podgorica, and the radio systems as well as by electro-magnetic waves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me one more thing. Let's clarify that do you know that all the connections that went outside the country went through Belgrade, the capital of the former Yugoslavia, all the connections to Europe would first flow to Europe; and then from Belgrade they could be transferred outside, farther out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not quite correct. There were international connections, connections with foreign countries went via Belgrade and via Zagreb and to a limited extent also via Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, what I'm saying is the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Yes, that is in the transcript. We're not going to deal in detail why coaxial cable is important and how many simultaneous telephone conversations you can conduct by using such a cable. We are going to talk about these radio relay system of communication. Can you please try to explain to the Chamber and the Prosecutors what happens and what sort of electronic equipment you need, what happens to human speech that needs to be transferred to a -- some sort of electronic signal, then you need to conduct this signal via oscillators, and so on. You don't have to be overly expert on this, but can we find out how sensitive and complicated this and how expensive it is if there is any degree of destruction at any section of the network from the source of energy, antennas, the transformation of voice into the signal, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is quite complex. I'm going to try to be as simple as I can, but in principle if we're talking about connections between specific telephone exchanges they are effected in two ways -- actually, not in two ways. There are two kinds of apparatus, one type is transmission equipment and the other type are multiplex equipment. Transmission equipment is used to convey a certain signal from one location to another so that you can use just regular cable, symmetrical cable, coaxial cable, or optical cable for these purposes, and you can have radio connections, radio relay connections, and satellite connections, so that is the transmission part. And the transmission equipment is also different according to its capacity. They can only be able to cover one telephone call or tens of thousands of telephone calls simultaneously. In order to have -- to be able to have several telephone conversations at the same time, you have the so-called multiplex devices where several speakers or speakers' telephone cables are connected to a device, the device can mix them all, and at the out -- exit you have just one cable where all of those are merged. Then you have the analog system and you have the digital system in this sense. At that time we were still using the so-called analog system. Today this is an outdated system and the digital system, the multiplex and radio relay devices, are used; coaxial cable is not used so much; optical fibre cable is used now in order to be able to transmit at large distances. I don't know if I answered. I mean it took a while, but...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are very sensitive, very complicated devices in all kinds of ways, and the radio relay cables are laid underground. The coaxial cable that we're talking about is laid along the railway tracks. I worked in the PTT, and because of that, the fact that the cable is laid down along the railway tracks, especially when the railway tracks are supplied with electricity, then that is threatened in several ways because of bridges, overpasses, underpasses, and different effects of the currents that are -- can be found around those railway tracks. As for the radio relay devices, they would need to be at prominent positions. They would need to have towers and these large antennas need to be placed there, the dish antennas, which can be quite large. In order to cover a certain area you would need to have at tops of hills or mountains some kind of relay station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to hear this part about the signals entering at one end and being mixed at the other and coming out as a single cable at the other, and this is all a complicated process. This is what I wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The second thing, when the signal is being transmitted from one device to the other, it's very important to know here if there is the possibility of deviation or curvature of such a signal, can it curve around a hill depending on the type of waves that are being used? Why is it essential to have optical visibility between one device that is transmitting the signal and the other one that would receive or amplify the signal?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these purposes we're using devices that operated extremely high frequencies, these are ultra-short wave-lengths, also high-frequency waves which are measured in gigahertz, and in this case this idea of curvature is out of the question, there has to be absolutely -- visibility, optical visibility, between the two points that are being connected and there has to be a short distance between these points. The greater the capacity, the distance is reduced. In the case when we have smaller capacities, then you can use, instead of the relay stations, some kind of passive, what we call a mirror, which redirects the signal in the same way that a mirror would redirect a beam of light. So because you have to have this visibility, if you want to go from Mostar outside, at that time we found a relay station at a location near Stolac on a hill called Hrgud at the Paric elevation, and that's where the base station was built. It was connected up and the connection from Mostar towards Podgorica and towards Split was transmitted via that station. At that time the station was, let's say, in the Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, all this is very technical, but I'm trying to bring this back to our problem, the problem we'll have to solve and we'll have to decide on regarding military issues. When a military unit, ex-unit, for example, is on the field, and this military unit is supposed to contact its chain of command, the communications system of these military units through radio -- I believe that at the time unless you had satellite phones you communicated with radio systems. So does this automatically imply the need for relay stations or these passive mirrors, as you called them? In other words, when you have a military communications system, does that mean that in the territory covered you need to have relay stations? Or is there a possibility for the military to use talkie-walkies or for another system to communicate from one unit to another without going through radio waves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I spoke here about the telecommunications system used by telecommunications companies, at least at that time. I didn't speak here about military uses or military equipment that is used by units of the military in the field. This is completely different type of equipment, and I can say something about that too if required. But we talked about the telecommunications system used by all citizens and the business community as well as some military units to a certain extent in this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also focused here on the witness clarifying the three things that are in the indictment, that the right side was responsible for cutting electricity or that the HVO can be blamed for the television signal being cut or for telephone lines being cut, and so on. I think everything about that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I want to ask you just one more thing. The coaxial cable laid down next to the railway tracks - and we will look at the two bridges which were knocked down - how many places near Sarajevo were not either under the control of the HVO or the B&H army were places where these cables were laid?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The period of 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the period before Mostar was, let's say, liberated from the Yugoslav Army, then it can be said that from Mostar to the north for a considerable distance the cable was in some way blocked or threatened. I just need to mention one more thing. The coaxial cable, it doesn't mean that you have electronic equipment in Mostar and electronic equipment in Sarajevo. It is of such a nature that you need to have an amplifier each few kilometres, and these nodes need to be supplied with electricity from the network. In some sections the electricity supply came from the end users, but in between it had to receive an electricity supply from somewhere. So the Sarajevo end did receive electricity from the area that was closer to Mostar, but the area that was immediately close to Sarajevo depended on the Serbian forces. But we knew that it was not possible to provide electricity to Sarajevo from Mostar. This is something that we saw and that we knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me go back to the telephone systems. Earlier we talked about electricity. Let's talk about the telephone system. We have on the ELMO this drawing made by General Praljak on the telephone network. I see that when you want -- when you're in Mostar you want to call Zagreb, you have to go through Sarajevo. If from Mostar you're calling Paris or Geneva, you have to go through Sarajevo and Belgrade. Now, given this drawing, let's assume that Mostar is isolated suddenly; then, according to you, technically if someone in Sarajevo blocks the system or bypasses or derogates the system, I would like to know whether in Mostar it totally -- the communication is cut. If someone in Sarajevo or, maybe also in Belgrade, decides to disturb or tamper with the telephone line, I'd like to know whether it's technically possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I would like to clarify this a little bit. You can see that there is a large telecommunications system in Mostar branching out in three directions: Sarajevo, Podgorica, and Split. At that time if the coaxial cable went down in any way, whether it was -- it was switched off or out of order, we had an alternative solution via the other two systems, Split or Titograd, to communicate with the rest of the country or with abroad. The only problem -- in fact, even if two segments were down, again we were able to communicate with the whole area of the former Yugoslavia and with abroad because, as I pointed out earlier, Zagreb also had links to abroad. The only problem was when all three segments were down, in that case Mostar and the surrounding area was no longer connected with the rest of the world. And that's what happened to us. It was not only Hrgud that fell which caused disruption to the radio relay system towards Split and Titograd, but there was another problem, the equipment in the building itself was damaged and so were the bridges, the bridges were knocked down, so we were completely cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, does this mean that General Praljak's drawing is not comprehensive? Because if you want to communicate with the rest of Europe or with the world from Mostar, if you can't go through Sarajevo or Titograd because they're down, you can go through Split. So on this drawing, shouldn't he have also added world and Europe at level of Split and Titograd? Isn't that missing from the drawing? Unless I'm mistaken, but if I've understood you right, I thought that if it doesn't go through to Sarajevo on the coaxial cable, you've got a back-up system either through Split or through Titograd. That's what I understood anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this sketch tells us something about the situation in Mostar, but this is just a part of the overall system. At that time Split was linked with Zagreb, Zagreb was linked with Belgrade, and Titograd had another link with Belgrade, so there were all kinds of communication lines in place. The schematic would be much more complex. I myself cannot now explain each and every detail of it. But since Mostar had only three systems in place: Coaxial cable towards Sarajevo and two wireless radio relay systems that went through the relay station at Paric, and when we couldn't use Paric or when the cable was down for whatever reason, on purpose, if it lost power or if it sustained any damage, we in Mostar were cut off, not only Mostar with the rest of the world but also Mostar with the region, the rest of the region, we could not communicate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: His Honour Antonetti asked you a somewhat different question. Assuming that Hrgud, where this relay station was located, that went then went on to the Biokovo relay station and on to Split; is that correct --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. No, no, not Biokovo but near Plejin Vrh near Posusje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Near Posusje. But assuming that Hrgud was not in Serb hands, as you indicated, even if Split could be reached, His Honour Antonetti asked whether the Split exchange had the ability to communicate with Europe or if it had to go through Zagreb and some channels. But I am doubtful about the time when Zagreb was allowed to have direct links with abroad by Belgrade because Madam Holjevac, a friend of mine, was in charge of development there. But can you tell me whether Podgorica and Split in the former Yugoslavia had direct links with abroad or if it had to go -- well, let's say partially through Zagreb but mainly through Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really tell you that with any certainty, but at the time when I worked in the PTT the communications with abroad - I know that because I know that Zagreb fought really hard to be given the right to communicate directly with at least some of the countries, but the moment you have a direct link with any given country you can then communicate with the rest of the world, but in the beginning Belgrade was the only node from which you could communicate with abroad. But later on Zagreb was allowed to have some links, and so did Ljubljana, but to a very limited scope. But I want to say that Split had very good links with Zagreb, Podgorica had very good -- a different kind of link with Belgrade through Serbia. So for them, losing this communication line through Mostar did not mean losing contact with, let's say, Belgrade. The capacity was somewhat reduced, but they could still have the communication lines that they had. If I knew that you would be asking me those questions, I would have prepared better and would have given you a better idea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, this is quite enough, thank you very much, about the struggle to establish communication lines with abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. In my view, it is not quite enough because I would like to know at what moment Zagreb was beginning to have contact with other countries. You said first and then you said later. That's a bit vague. Could you give an indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I spoke about the time-period while I was still an employee of the PTT. That was before 1978. At that time, at the time when I joined the PTT and I started working there, we did not have any automatic exchanges in our area at all, in Herzegovina. It was set up gradually, and as it was being set up the international lines were also set up. The first international lines were set up from Belgrade, but later on Zagreb managed to get some but that was all before the 1980s. At the time that we are now talking about, Zagreb definitely had communication lines with the rest of the world; I can say that. So if we in Mostar were able to reach Split, we were able to reach the rest of the world, provided their lines were up. And as far as I know, throughout the war in Croatia and in Dalmatia, they were able to maintain communication lines with Zagreb and were able to maintain the telephone traffic. There were minor disruptions but it was functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, with these corrections, could you please sign this sketch, put a date on it, and can we please have the IC number.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this sketch is quite clear to me, but if you're asking me if I'm being asked those questions, then somebody might say that this is actually not very good. I would need to make a proper schematic actually.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll just forget about it. Could you please look at the last sketch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need a number for this document on the Sarajevo-Belgrade-Titograd-Zagreb telephone schematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps it's useful to assure you, Witness, that when you sign this that does not mean that it is regarded as your testimony; it is just a formality because you have looked at it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the third sketch shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00852. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to Mr. Praljak on the relevance of this document. If I understood what our witness said, he was -- this was when he was working in the PTT and that was before 1980. I would like to know whether this schematic can be applied to the relevant period in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this question. There were no major changes in relation to this schematic in the period before the war. It was only during the war and after the war. The whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a network of optic fibre cables put in, so now the situation is quite different. But at that time this was new equipment that was functioning quite well that hasn't been depreciated yet, so that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We will agree that if we disregard the links with Belgrade and Ljubljana and Zagreb and then abroad, that the essence here is the radio links through Hrgud to Split and in whose hands those facilities were. Could we please look at the last schematic. This is a rough outline of Mostar, eastern Mostar, the Neretva River, the western Mostar, and the Spanish square, Tito's bridge, Sant iceva Street, and there at Bulevar you can see the building where the telephone exchange was and all the other facilities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please take a pen or I can give you a pen, could you please indicate how the coaxial cable was laid from the post building. You can see the customs bridge here. Could you please just draw this in.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So it crossed the customs bridge to the left bank of the river Neretva and then to the north then to the railway bridge and it folded back and went north. My question to you is whether in 1992 whether those two bridges were blown up. We're not going to be talking about other bridges.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 both of those bridges and other bridges were blown up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Another question. The other telephone installations from the post building, post office, to the eastern part of Mostar, did they go underneath the bridges?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, practically across every bridge in Mostar there were all kinds of cables, with the exception of the Old Bridge. As the city developed, the larger cables were set up, larger-capacity cables, and they were laid exclusively across the bridges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And so once the bridges were torn down, this all collapsed too?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please initial this. This has no meaning at all. This does not mean that this is your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The fourth sketch shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00853. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Our last topic, it's television signal. Let us assume that Sarajevo Radio and Television has enough power and broadcasts a strong signal from its powerful aerials. Now, can this signal be received in Mostar without any other equipment, relay equipment?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot be seen in Mostar without relay facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what is the frequency of the signal, how strong must it be, is there any curvature, or does it need to be linear, whether the repeater at Velez was the prerequisite for the signal to be received in Mostar from Sarajevo, not only the one in Velez but the repeaters that were also in Serb hands. So could you please explain all this to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TV signal - and there's also the audio for the -- to coincide with the video signal - requires a broad spectrum in order to be transmitted, and the transmission has to be high quality because it is such a broad spectrum. And this can be transmitted using high-frequency equipment. The equipment is actually similar to the equipment used for voice transmission. Sarajevo did broadcast its signal to Bjelasnica. There was a relay station there and it had a very, very strong TV signal transmitter that covered this whole area. As for Mostar itself, it was covered from Velez but that was not sufficient because Mostar is in the shadow of Velez so to speak so that only parts of western Mostar received the signal from Velez, which is why even before the war there was a small station, Planinica which was where the TV signal was broadcast into Mostar. Similar small relay facilities were set up in other areas to ensure the reception of the video signal throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the moment when the signal at Velez was out, Mostar lost its feed, video feed, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: First question: How tall was the tower at Velez with all the dishes as they're colloquially known? There were quite a few things up there. How tall was it, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time I worked in the PTT when this facility was being constructed. It is a very tall tower. I can't give you the exact figure now, but I think that it is at least 35 metres tall. But it's a really massive tower. It was done -- it was built using steel, it's tubular design, and it had to be done like that because Bjelasnica and Velez relay stations are at very great height, Velez is about 2.000 metres and Bjelasnica even more than that. So in winter-time, the conditions there are quite impossible, wind, ice, snow. So the aerials on Velez were actually protected using special equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, and you have to have power sources?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you recall when you no longer could see the tower at Velez - and you will agree that Velez is the mountain that goes up on the east side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped seeing it in June or maybe July 1992, that was the time when the Yugoslav forces pulled out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we can say that when they lost the battle, when they were in retreat, that the -- after that time this tower was no longer there. Tell me something else, if we take as a hypothesis that Velez remained in place and that Bjelasnica was gone, we agree then that sometime in July or June 1992 this was torn down, this was destroyed, this tower?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could no longer see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Another question. Now let us take as a hypothesis that all this equipment at Velez for the reception of the signal to the western side, and then you had to put something in place for the eastern side because it was in the shadow although it was above Mostar, although there can be no curvature if you have such a high-frequency signal; if the buildings are in the shadow they cannot receive the signal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's assume that everything is all right at Velez, but, for example, that Bjelasnica is in the Serb hands, the Army of Republika Srpska, and had any kind of strong signal been broadcast could this signal have been received at Velez?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not have been. The only possibility was that possibly it could be sent from some other elevation, but right now I cannot say that any elevation existed. The Velez location received its signal from Bjelasnica, the antennas were directed towards Bjelasnica so it was not simple just to turn them somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's look at three more documents and then we will be done, document 1D 02670, 1D 02670. You saw the document yesterday and the sketch that you signed is something that accompanies this document. I would just like you to look together with me at the document. We see that it was signed by Enes Santic, an electrical engineer, and can we look at the first page of the Croatian text where it says that Mostar was a key communications centre before the war and that it had experts for design and construction and that it was possible to set up a certain connection with the help of experts. Is it possible that all those connections with the technical and financial generous help of Republic of Croatia -- that's how it was done, that all those connections were set up with the technical and financial help?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that at that time when Mostar lost its connections with western Herzegovina, it was essential to link the locations in western Herzegovina to Split; and this could have been done by using existing equipment and by changing the location of that equipment to a certain extent. Also, the reserve equipment could be used that was at the disposal of the PTT and the spare equipment of UNIS PTT which relocated its equipment from the factory, transferred it to western Herzegovina, and had some options to do something in that regard. The HPT Zagreb, the Croatian PTT, especially the telecommunications centre at Split, at that time did assist for all of that to be finished and completed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to read just a couple of things for you. It says: "According to the estimates, the damage on PTT elements systems and equipment only in Mostar are valued at $28 million US." Would you agree with this estimate?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was written by Mr. Enes Santic. At the time we were not even able to go about attempting to assess the actual situation, but it's a fact that a telephone exchange of 14.000 connections was completely burned. There was not a single part of it that could be used. The antennas were completely destroyed, the antenna poles were destroyed. As for the rest of the equipment, we didn't know what state it was in. It was damaged and it would have required months of work by qualified personnel, qualified personnel, it's something that we could not have done without the help of the Ericsson factory in Zagreb, the Nikola Tesla factory, which installed those exchanges. As for other equipment we needed UNIS's assistance and the help of other suppliers like Italian, German suppliers like Siemens, Nera from Norway, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have used one hour and five minutes already. I suppose, therefore, that the other Defence teams won't have any questions for this witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, no others will have questions so I'm going to finish quickly with a couple of more documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The next document in the series is 1D 02671, also signed by Santic whom you said that you know. He says in the first sentence: "The telecommunications building in Mostar was severely damaged after a number of days of bombing. Scores of missiles or shells that fell on this building and close to the building caused damage to the roof and side walls ..." and so on and so forth. In the fourth paragraph it says: "The telecommunications systems suffered complete damage," which you confirmed. And then on page 2 in the Croatian text he says in Article C: "We are currently working to set up telephone communications with Siroki Brijeg, and for that purpose we are assembling a 12-channel device. Via Siroki Brijeg it will be possible to establish the connection with western Herzegovina and Dalmatia." Can you please tell us, is it correct that a coaxial cable was installed overhead towards Mostar, and then that supported an entire exchange?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to explain very briefly. At that point in time, Mostar lost all communications because of major damage with its neighbours and with the world. The only option we had at the time was to lay coaxial -- actually, regular cable, it wasn't even coaxial cable at the time, from Siroki Brijeg to Mostar, and we had to use wooden poles and surface ground to lay this cable. We had no time to dig it in. It was not possible to do it either because at the time there was still the danger of shelling. So in this way Mostar was secured with first just temporary connections, we installed a manual telephone switchboard, we returned 40 years back, and connected this manual switchboard to Siroki Brijeg and connected it also to a private house telephone exchange of the Ministry of the Interior. And we set up the most essential connections in that way, and then we proceeded step by step to improve this system on a daily basis. I'm just talking about the sequence of events now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we look at the last document 1D 02672, it's a report of the 30th of June, 1997. This is what I can see, 07, so 1997. On the first page at the bottom, in the last third of the Croatian text, it says: "In order to provide for any kind of communications, aerial telephone cable was laid down quickly in the direction Mostar-Siroki Brijeg ..." and so on and so forth. And then it says: "At the time the only possibility of communicating with the world was via Split through a specially built system and mobile stations of the telecommunications system from Croatia that could have been used in limited areas covered by the signal from Biokovo." You already testified about that. I think there's nothing disputable about that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And at the bottom it says: "The Split telecommunications centre donated a telephone switchboard with a capacity of 480 connections, which was installed in a truck." Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 2 towards the end of the first third on the text on the page it says: "By persistent work and efforts of the staff and with the help of the UNIS Mostar and Nikola Tesla staff, and especially the telecommunications centre Split, we managed to establish communications ..." and so on and so forth. Do you also agree -- well, we have no reason --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I actually wrote that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Just one more thing, please. The Nikola Tesla factory which manufactured most of the telecommunication equipment parts before the war began and during the war only had business and technical cooperation with Ericsson. Ericsson was not an owner of Nikola Tesla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So Ericsson became the owner of a major part of the Nikola Tesla capital only after the war in Croatia ended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. We tried to clarify things a little bit and I thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, the best thing to do would be to have the usual break now, following which the Prosecutor can start with his cross-examination. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, good afternoon. And to all those in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Kozulj. You've already been asked questions by Mr. Karnavas, so you are familiar with the format, if you will, in terms of when we speak different languages there will often be a bit of a pause, perhaps, in the courtroom between the two of us speaking waiting for translation to catch up with each of us. My pause is not necessarily an invitation for you to speak more, but we just have to allow the interpreters to catch up with both of us. I also will be showing you exhibits in the same way that Mr. Karnavas was showing them to you. The two binders have already been made available to you. I will also be making reference to some of the Defence exhibits that were used yesterday, the so-called 1D exhibits, and we'll have to figure out the easiest way for you to find those, if you want to use the same notebook that Mr. Karnavas provided to you yesterday or some other means, or of course we always have e-court. But I hope that in every instance you will be able to find the document that I'm referring to and the usher will also be assisting us. Mr. Kozulj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge is kindly requested to switch off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kozulj, I'd like to go straight to the topic of the Special-Purposes Council. For these purposes you may wish to have in front of you Exhibit P 00190, which is in binder 1, the Prosecution binder. They should all be -- in the Prosecution binders you should be able to find them -- all the exhibits in numerical order I hope. Generally, at least in the Prosecution binder - no offence intended - you'll find the English document or translation on top and the Serbo-Croatian document following it. So if you could please look at P 00190. Now, I think everyone in the courtroom has seen this before. This is when you and a number of other persons were appointed to this thing called the council for special purposes and on the 7th of May, 1992. Just briefly, do you recall any discussion leading up to the formation of that counsel? And I'm not asking now for the circumstances about the war. I think we all have a pretty good idea of what was happening in May of 1992 at this point with the JNA and with the Serb forces in the Mostar vicinity. So I'm not talking about those circumstances. I'm just asking if you can assist the Judges with any information about the discussion or debate or dialogue that went on around this time about the formation of this body called the Special-Purposes Council.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was a discussion about it or not. All I know is that I personally did not participate in such a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was dealing with technical matters at the time to help people working in telecommunications to prepare for what was evidently coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you may have mentioned this but it wasn't entirely clear to me then. So how was it then that you came to know that you were on this council? Did someone hand you this document or give you a phone call or come to your office? How did you find out that, Mr. Kozulj, you are now on the Special-Purposes Council?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of these people were people that I met on a daily basis. At the time I didn't have an office because my office in Mostar was located on the east side, and at the time the east side of Mostar was already a place where it was very difficult to move around. I received this information, I don't know exactly from whom, but from someone from this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the people that are on the list, besides yourself, starting at the top of the list with Mr. Tomic and Mr. Prlic and others, is there anyone on that list that you had not had prior substantial dealings with?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew all these people from before. I'm not sure about Mr. Vidan Raspudic, I'm not sure if I knew him earlier. As for all the others, I know them all very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me just go back again to your coming on this board. So do I understand correctly - and if I'm wrong, please correct me or elaborate - that you -- just someone came to you on the street as best you can remember and you found out that you had been placed on this body. Did anyone ask you if you were interested in serving or said, We'd like to invite you to come on this board? Or can you tell us anything more about that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I openly made it known to all the people that I encountered that I was placing myself at the disposal and with my knowledge and experience I would like to help considering the situation that Mostar found itself in. This was something that everyone knew, and it was probably the reason why somebody put my name forward and why Mr. Tomic appointed me to this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's talk about the -- another document that you saw, and it may be that we don't have to look at all these documents because you've seen them just yesterday. One is the document that I think you looked at which was the 15th of May, 1992, decision to create the Mostar Municipal Staff, and the -- or coming out of -- the one that was disbanding the earlier Crisis Staff, P 00209. But you may recall you were asked some questions yesterday about particular language in that document, and I don't want to talk about the whole document because I do want to try to move fairly quickly. But in paragraph 3 of that order, it talks about the fact that: "Until the government referred to in paragraph 2 of this order is formed, the Special-Purpose Council of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens." And I recall when you were discussing this yesterday, Mr. Kozulj, that you indicated that you thought that was unrealistic, that mandate, if you will, as discussed in item 3, that the Special-Purpose Council would take this on was unrealistic. I put it to you, please, whether it was realistic or not is not so much the issue, but is that not in fact the instructions that were given in the decision of the 15th of May, 1992, those responsibilities would fall to the Special-Purpose Council, realistic or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't explain a little bit earlier, even though you don't allow me to explain the situation in town, but I would like to say this. I read many books about war and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and only from two of them I understood what the war actually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my question to you - is not about the war, we've heard a lot about that, we've heard two years of that - my question is: That's what the document marked as that exhibit and that decision, that's what it says, did it not. Whether you thought it was realistic or not -- maybe it was realistic, but that was the mandate given to the Special-Purposes Council; correct? If I'm reading the language wrong or you think it's been mistranslated, tell me. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that that is what it says and that is so in this order, but also I understand it to mean that we were obliged to do this job or to propose a way that it should be done and this is what we did. This is what I take from this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you go next, please, to 1D -- this will be a Defence -- it won't be in that binder, sir, you'll have to go to one of the -- either on the e-court or the Defence binder, 1D 02743. It may be in our -- let me just double-check. You have that, sir, and it seems to me that looking over in your direction you do. This is a document around the same time-period concerning the creation of these -- or the performance, if you will, of these various services and functions. And it says that: "The Special-Purpose Council of the Municipal Staff of HVO Mostar, at the sessions held on 15 and 19 May 1992, in considerations about the functioning of essential services in the town and municipality, has concluded that the vital services of the state administration and functioning of the town have not been adjusted, in terms of quality, to the war conditions in Mostar." I'm not going to read the entire thing to you, sir, because everyone in the courtroom, including you, has it in front of you. Next paragraph, among other things, refers to the municipal executive bodies. Aren't all those things, sir, the essential services, the administration, and functioning of the town, the municipal executive bodies, aren't those the things that we call government?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say this about this document. This document is not signed. This is a rough draft that one of us in the Special-Purpose Council made on the basis of the discussion we had regarding the task that we were given according to the decision by Jadran Topic. We absolutely knew that we were not able to do it, and that is why we discussed a proposal for President Topic, how the civilian authority in the town of Mostar could be organized in those conditions. This is a rough draft and it's an impetus to him and his associates to shape that into some kind of decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you would agree with me then, sir, that this document describes the functions of the government of this town of Mostar, essential services, administration and functioning of the town, municipal executive bodies, those are the functions of government?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a correction. This document is just thoughts on paper on how the municipal authority in Mostar could function. This is just our thinking. It's not a document that was adopted -- I don't know, we have some other documents later which define ways in which the authority was ultimately constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go next, please, to 1D 02715. This is, I believe -- is and again, many of these, sir, you will have seen and I'm just taking you back through them to ask some, if you will, follow-up questions. This is the document which was appointing you a member in fact of the Special-Purposes Council, and it's an appointment issued over the name of someone called Jasmin Jaganjac who is described here as commander. And if I'm not mistaken, you described him yesterday as a military commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the HVO staff in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you consider that this was a military appointment?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider this appointment of the commander of the HVO of me as a person to help the command in matters which are my professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So did you consider yourself by this appointment to be acting in a military capacity?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When Commander Jaganjac issued this appointment naming you to the Special-Purpose Council, did you understand that Mr. Jaganjac was acting in a civilian role or as a military role?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Jaganjac was acting here in his military capacity and that he engaged me as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, we saw a number of documents yesterday, and I'm not going to turn to them but just in case anyone's curious, I have in mind as examples 1D 02714, 1D 02666, which again were described as orders. I think most of us tended to think of them -- if someone issues an order, tend to think of that as a military matter. Is it common in your experience around this time that when these types of instruction or appointments were made it was the order coming from people like Mr. Jaganjac?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this terminology was normally used because it was a war, so this term was used regardless of who was actually issuing the document because there was a need to stress that the task in question had to be done. In wartime, that's at least -- that's my experience and that's how I see it. There are no recommendations or no advice, there are only tasks that are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you please to next look at 1D 00906.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is again around the same time-period, 20 May 1992, it is also described as an order issued by someone named Mladen Zulj, which I believe is a name that we've heard before and we will hear again in connection with the PTT. In this order which Mr. Zulj says for the HVO, chief coordinator of PTT services of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Zulj issues an order to -- it says PTT units in Grude, Ljubuski, and following. And in item number 1: "All PTT units shall, according to given (present) number of channels, secure an unobstructed communication between PTT Centres according to the wartime technical criterion of PTT connections, namely in the ratio of 1:5 (one channel = five subscribers). "2. Directors of PTT units shall arrange the disconnection according to this criterion through the HVO command ..." Let me stop there for a moment. If we look at the top left corner of the document or in the letterhead, if you will, we see again this is coming from HVO main headquarters on the 20th of May, 1992. Did you understand Mr. Zulj to have military powers to be able to issue orders for the HVO issuing from the HVO main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj was appointed the coordinator for post and telecommunications by the president of the HZ HB. He was a civilian. He did civilian work. This is an order that pertains to the civilian sphere of those activities, but this was probably done pursuant to an approval of the president of the HZ HB that we had in writing, that Mr. Zulj issued this kind of order, which in my opinion was a necessity at the time. And if you allow me, I would like to explain. At that time when the state was in disarray, when Bosnia and Herzegovina had broken down, when there was a great deal of damage to the telecommunications capacities in Mostar, something needed to be done in order to establish the telecommunication lines and to maintain them. Order -- orders had to be issued because some managers in PTT units, which were deep in the free territory, acted in such a way that they did not want to assist others who found themselves in difficulties. So there was this necessity for somebody to issue an order to them to do something in light of solidarity with others to switch off some of their capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We're going to come back and I'll tell everyone in the courtroom - including Your Honours - that we're going to come back to the content of the order in a few minutes. But right now I'm focusing more on the order, it's the fact of the order itself and where it came from, but you agree with me, sir, that this order was issued by Mr. Zulj describing himself as acting for the HVO and issuing from the HVO main headquarters? You agree with me on that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree because that's what it says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but at that time the HVO was both civilian and military authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly the point that I was coming to, sir. Isn't the effect of what you were telling us yesterday and what you've told us again these last few minutes that the situation in Mostar, in Herzegovina, at that time was we are talking about a mixed civilian/military war-time government, weren't we?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't now say whether it is this thing or the other. I just know that at that time initiative had to be taken by people themselves, taking initiative, doing things on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it was the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, again it's probably a problem with the interruption -- with the translation, my apology. But, sir, you just said a moment ago the HVO was both civilian and military authority, and then you said Well, people were taking it on their own initiative. Sir, I've just shown you a number of documents, they were orders, they were orders, and you just said a few moments ago, I believe you said, that everyone had to act in these conditions, and whether it was Mr. Jaganjac acting in a military capacity or a civilian capacity, these things had to be done because it was war-time conditions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way you phrase it. Jaganjac was acting in the military aspect and Zulj in the civilian aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in this situation --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that situation, sir, and what you've again described to us the last few minutes, wasn't it the case that many of the distinctions which might exist in a more peacetime environment between the civilian government and the military, those distinctions were blurred, weren't they, and some people were exercising both civilian and military power?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me for a specific person, whether they were military or civilian, I can give you my opinion. I don't know whether some of them were both. That's not what I was dealing with. Throughout the war what I wanted to do was to commit myself to helping people in the areas where I had the expertise. Now, whether the order to do so came from a military person or a civilian person or whether no orders had come at all because I did lots of things on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So are you telling the Judges, sir, that you didn't care whether the order came from a civilian or a military person or both, it didn't really matter to you and you didn't make a distinction?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that I didn't care. It just didn't matter so much to me. What mattered to me was the task that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you look next, please, at 1D 02716, 1D 02716. This is a certificate issued on the 9th of May, 1992, by the HVO -- it's actually described here as the Herceg-Bosna Main Staff. Did you know Mr. Zadro, who apparently issued this certificate?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Zadro before this order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know him later?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met him because Mr. Zulj, who was the coordinator, authorised such by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, asked me to assist and wanted me to meet Mr. Zadro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And when you received this certificate from Mr. Zadro, he was an officer in the HVO military; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So again, did you consider this certificate to be a military order, had you been given this permission by the military, or was Mr. Zadro acting in some other capacity?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This certificate is important because it accords me freedom of movement. I am issued a certificate to the effect that because of -- but for the purpose of establishing communication lines, I am allowed to move freely in the territory controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you will please go back to the document we started with, and that is P 00190, the Special-Purposes Council document, in the Prosecution binder, P 00190, the first binder. If I can direct your attention, please, to the fourth numbered paragraph where it says: "Work shall be coordinated through Messrs. Neven Tomic, Jadranko Prlic, and Borislav Puljic, exclusively with the president of the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff, Mr. Jadran Topic." Could we correctly understand this, sir, is that of this Special-Purposes Council, that Mr. Tomic, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Puljic, formed or acted as a sort of executive committee?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could take it to mean that they were coordinators in the Special-Purpose Council and that they coordinated the work of all of us, the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it says that they should conduct this activity exclusively with the president of the Mostar HVO -- excuse me, Municipal Staff, Mr. Topic. Do you know why that was? What was the purpose of apparently making this very clear if that was to be exclusively with Mr. Topic?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, was there some other body that potentially was -- had some sort of a parallel organization or making other similar efforts to do these things? Was there something about that that Mr. Topic wanted to make it very clear that these people would deal only with him?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you that I don't know why he said it that way. He probably wanted to have some insight into what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to next go, please, to the Exhibit P 00578 in the Prosecution binder, first binder. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, I'm still looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be the minutes of a meeting of the HVO HZ HB held on the 14th of October, 1992, with such people in attendance, Mr. Prlic, president; Mr. Zubak; Mr. Buntic; Mr. Stojic; Mr. Tomic; and others. And if you will turn to -- for the English readers in the courtroom it will be on page 6 of the English document. If you can find part of the document, sir, I'm trying to assist you which it says item 6. It isn't item 6 that I'm looking for now, but if you find item 6 and you go directly below that item, after that numbered item, until you see it, a discussion where it says: "Mr. President proposed adopting a decision to appoint acting director, president, and members of the managing board of the HZ HB PTT ..." You see that now? I believe it's the fourth page of the Serbo-Croatian version. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about item 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It follows after item 6, sir. Unfortunately, it's a part of the minutes that doesn't particularly flow well in terms of the numbering. I don't believe it is item 6, but it follows after item 6 and above a section called "conclusions." It should be on page 4 of the Serbo-Croatian document, sir. And if I'm mistaken, I'm sorry, but it's on page 6 of the English document. You may find it on the bottom of page 3 I'm told now.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, it says that -- thank you. It says that: "Mr. President proposed adopting a decision to appoint" these persons, and under that we see Mr. Mladen Zulja as nominated to be acting director of the Herceg-Bosna PTT. I take it, sir, that is in fact the same Mladen Zulja that we saw on the document a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then following that is the nomination of the president and members of the managing board. You are nominated as president and then the following four individuals are proposed as members of the -- other members of the managing board; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in terms of Mr. Zulja, it says that he was being named at that time acting director. Is there any particular reason why he was being named acting director as opposed to director?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a public company, post and telecommunications, established pursuant to a government decision, the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And it is usual practice to appoint the board of directors to appoint the acting director, and then they go on to draft the statute of the company; and then this statute is submitted to the founder, which in this case is the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, for its approval. Only then is the director formally appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, the translation that we're getting in the last few minutes about this was a public company, but just so there's no confusion, was the PTT that's being formed here, is that something that we've also described in the last couple of days as a public enterprise? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Javno poduzeca," public company or enterprise. I don't know how you could translate it best, but that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
