utterances.text: And it was -- was Mr. President or Mr. Prlic who was making these proposals, according to the top of this page 6, and again do you recall whether Mr. Prlic had approached you sometime prior to the 14th of October, 1992, to ask you, Are you interested in doing this? I'm going to put your name forward at the next government meeting? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having discussed this with Mr. Prlic, but I did discuss it with Mr. Vlado Soljic. In the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, he was the minister of industry and economy. We talked about a need to establish public companies and we agreed that in this public company, the post and telecommunications of the HZ HB, I should become the chairman of the board of directors and I accepted that. And probably then Mr. Soljic discussed this with President Prlic and they tabled this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just -- if I may just interrupt and I apologise. Perhaps Mr. Scott misspoke, but if you do look at the document it says that the president proposed adopting a decision; it does not say, not that there's anything nefarious in it, that the president proposed the particular names. He proposed adopting the decision. How the names were placed on that decision, that's something else. So I just want to make sure that that's clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look down further into the minutes below the names of the four other individuals nominated for the board other than yourself, in addition to yourself, you'll see that another member of the government, Mr. Kvesic apparently objected to this procedure and did not feel that this was an appropriate way to make appointments. Did that issue ever come to your attention? Did anyone ever tell you around this time that, Well, an issue was raised at the government meeting about how we should do this and whether you should be appointed and how that should be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, again I'm going to object. If you look very closely, he objects because... and then he says, according to the information he has, keeping in mind that Kvesic, in his position, he was minister of the interior at the time -- the head of the department of interior at the time, and of course he probably had some information as to why those two individuals should not be appointed. Again, I'm going to ask that if we're going to be posing questions that we be somewhat precise with the language that's in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- it's a fair -- absolutely a fair reading of the document. The document is in front of everyone. It says that he objected as against the decision to appoint the board, especially but -- to the whole board, and then he goes on to say in principle he does not accept this method of election. So I don't want to be accused of mis-characterizing the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did this issue ever come to your attention, that there had been some dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, the Trial Chamber will find it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nobody said anything to me or needed to say anything to me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how soon after the 14th of October did you find that you had, in fact, been appointed the managing director of the -- or president, if you will, president of the managing board? Did someone call you later that same day or how did you find out that this action had been taken?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this -- these minutes before, and from what I can see that's written there is that the appointment of the president and the members of the managing board of the public enterprise PTT HZ HB is being left for the next meeting of the Government of Herceg-Bosna. I or the others did not see this, but nobody needed to inform me about it or let me know about it. When I was actually appointed, that's when I was informed of it and that's when I began to carry out those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question, sir, was: When was that? When did you find out that you had been placed in this position?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't remember when you took up these responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a formal question. The entire time from the moment the situation deteriorated in our area, I worked together with people, helped them, made suggestions, and in some way tried to help --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it was just a formal appointment, the official appointment, it wasn't that important to me. I really don't remember when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned several times you were trying to do things to help people and no one's questioning that at this point. But I just want to be clear on this, so you considered this appointment a formality; is that what the Judges should understand?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Please. I -- well, the appointment to this post implies a certain kind of work. There was a duty at the time as well as a responsibility. Up until then, all I had were some -- some duties, but I didn't have any real responsibilities. I had a kind of advisory role to help people to work. From the point in time when I was appointed president of the management board, I then was given considerable duties and then it was no longer a formal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in going forward then with your work on behalf of or as the managing president of the board, excuse me, did you in fact work with Mr. Zulja as director and did he then, as you said a few moments ago, did he also become the director as opposed to acting director? If not, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I continued to work with Mr. Zulj, and when the managing board was appointed I was its president and Mr. Zulj was appointed the director. He was no longer acting director but the director of the PTT of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you continue to then be the president of the board, of the managing board, and Mr. Zulja the director throughout the time that you were in that position until approximately mid-November 1993 when you became a minister in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was the president of the managing board. That's when I became that by a government appointment. I think at one of the subsequent meetings of the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna this is what happened, Herceg-Bosna, Zulj was the director of that public company and he was that until the point in time when a vacancy announcement was made public and a new director of the company was elected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in these public companies who has power in reality? Is it the president of the managing board or is it the director of this public company? At the time, I'm not talking about now, but at the time who has real power, is it the president of the managing board or is it the director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a very complex question. I said before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm asking that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... explain. What it means is that a public company is founded by some socio-political community, the municipality, a regional organization such as the HZ HB or the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The public enterprise or its managing board, together with the director and the services, prepares a statute of the company. The statute of the company precisely defines the tasks to be performed by the managing board, to be performed by the administration, and which jobs need to be given to the founders, the socio-economic community, so it is very clearly laid out who is in charge of what. So the managing board here has the obligation to adopt a plan, to adopt a report, especially the financial report, to adopt the organization of the company, the resolution of major issues such as investments, and then the administration carries out other matters, technical questions, employment, the allocation of staff. This is how these things were organized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on that, it actually flows from -- or at least I think it was related to that question. Who then -- who were you accountable to as the president of the managing board? Who did the board and you as the head of that board, who were you accountable to?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The managing board was responsible to the founder, and in this case this was the HZ HB government and it's primarily responsible to the minister, Mr. Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did you have any particular office locations or places where you and Mr. - perhaps separate or it may have been the same location, perhaps not - you and Mr. Zulja worked during this period from approximately October 1992 to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj is the director of the company and he is an employee of the company and he had an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was that located? Sir, where was it located, please?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately where in Mostar, can you give us an approximate location or address?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the Zrinski Sports Society Stadium in Mostar, because the premises of the PTT in Mostar at that time were unfit for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where -- did you have an office, sir, in connection with your function as the president of managing board?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president and members of the managing board are not employed in the company, they are not employed in the company. They don't have the duty of turning up to work every day, and they do not receive a salary for that like the employees do; they only work through meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So where were you -- did you have a business location or office that you went to during that time-period then in Mostar in -- from October 1992 to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an office. I didn't have an office, I didn't need an office. All the PTT public company offices of the HZ HB were at my disposal. But as I said before, the managing board worked through meetings. The president does not have any particular powers, he's one -- the first among equals and the materials for the meetings are prepared by the administration headed by the director, Mr. Zulj, and they are the ones who prepare everything that is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where were you residing during this time, sir? If you didn't have an office, where were you residing during the time October 1992 to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was residing at my apartment in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was approximately that location or address, please?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the street was called the street of Petar Drapsin, number 37, 88.000 Mostar. The street today is called Fra. Franjo Milicevica, Father Franjo Milicevic, 37, 88.000 Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see in the translation that it is Petar Trapcin. Actually it is Petar Drapsin, D-r-a-p-s-i-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, turning to the topic -- that whole topic of telephone service in particular, Judge Trechsel made a comment at some point along the way yesterday about -- I'm not saying this is an exact quote, so I hope you won't hold it against me if I'm not exactly dead on point, but something to the effect, was there a distinction between what might be called privileged communicators versus the general civilian population. Where I want to go from that, sir, isn't it correct that there was telephone service in Mostar and the surrounding area, it was just a question of how that service was allocated? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar was without communications -- I mean, it depends what period we are talking about -- oh, well, I'm sorry. I have to start from the beginning. Up until the time of the destruction of Mostar, Mostar had normal communications, they are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we don't have the time -- sir --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have limited time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, but there was no specificity in the question as to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then I'll restate the question. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, after the time where you say -- and it's been indicated that in approximately May of 1992 that the PTT building in Mostar was shelled and at least I believe what you've told us, if I'm not mistaken, is that between approximately May of 1992 and April of 1994 Mostar and Sarajevo were cut off in terms of telephone communication. So after that, after May 1992, I'm challenging you, sir, very transparent about that, it would be correct to understand, wouldn't it, that in fact during that time-period, though, just so we understand, there was telephone service and it existed in Mostar and the surrounding areas. You could call a lot of places in Bosnia, maybe Sarajevo or not. But it was a question of allocating the existing telephone service; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to try to explain briefly. For a very brief time Mostar did not have any communications, then gradually we set up communications and increased the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this time that you are talking about. Before that Mostar had --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the problem we had yesterday was that there was no -- often no specification of time-period. So you say there was a time when there was no communication in Mostar. So please tell us the time, give us dates. From when to when?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that the shelling of the PTT building as far as I can recall was on the 14th of May, 1999 -- no, 1992. We set up first communications some days after that, let's say a week after that, we established communications with the outside world. The first telephone exchange of a capacity of only 1 per cent of what we actually had before the war arrived in the form of a donation of the Split communications centre, and its capacity was 480 numbers. This was sometime in August 1992, if I remember correctly. It was summer in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go, please, to Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then these --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go to 1D 00566. 1D 00566, and I'll appreciate it, sir, if we can try to move as efficiently as possible because, again, my time is also limited. It's also on the screen, it may be faster for you. You saw this document yesterday -- you saw this document yesterday. Now, this relates to -- admittedly, this relates to electrical power, but this was the allocation of existing power-supply, who was to get it, on the -- as of the 19th of June, 1992, and you would agree with me, would you not, that some locations, government buildings, government facilities, military facilities, were given priority and in many instances on the list it says they would permanently have power. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For example, about two-thirds of the way down or a little below halfway down the list you have Municipal Staff, and the Municipal Staff would have power permanently; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a couple -- several lines down, just as one more example, I notice that the ham radio operators at Rondo, they had permanent power. Do you recall why the ham radio operators at Rondo had permanent power?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war conditions ham radio operators have enormous importance where communications are concerned between people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now -- so going back to telephone service, sir, what -- didn't the same exact process apply to the allocation of telephone service, you had 480 -- at least one point in time, soon after during the summer of 1992, you had something like at least 480 numbers or lines, and weren't those allocated in essentially a similarly way, essential offices, government functions, the military, were allocated telephone service; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to please go to P 06807, Prosecution binder, the first binder, binder number 1. If we can look at e-court, please. Can you look on the -- if you can't find it -- all right. Thank you very much. Sir, if you have P 06807, this is an order over the name of Bruno Stojic, at least the typed name of Bruno Stojic. There is no date on the document, but I submit to you the best we can do is that the number of the document bears a reference to 1992. But in this document, Mr. Stojic raises issues that says: "Based on the previous situation regarding telephone lines that are not satisfying our needs, and in order to improve them, especially for the needs of the "Main Staff" HVO and its units, as well as the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. "I order: "To reduce the number of telephone connections on the telephone central (connections that are in private houses)." Mr. Stojic in point 3 goes on to make it clear that the Herceg-Bosna defence department, in fact, is the exclusive owner of all telephone connections, et cetera. Do you see that? That accurately states the affairs at that time, does it not? An effort was being made -- perhaps the average person, if you will, living on the street didn't have telephone service, but the government leaders, the government and the military, did, didn't they? Mr. Stojic, among others, was making sure of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- well, I haven't seen this before, but I think I know what it's about. The public company, the HZ HB PTT, has its prices at which it operates and it charges for its services and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise to you. My question is not about price --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, unless the Chamber will allow me more time, my question has nothing to do with price; my question has to do with the allocation of lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if Mr. Scott was a little more precise in his questions he would get more precise answers. But if he asks wide questions, he's going to get a wide answer, and the gentleman is entitled to provide explanations, especially since he's being asked to comment on a document that he hasn't seen before. Now, yesterday there were at least two, maybe three, interventions by Judge Trechsel where he wanted to know whether the gentleman had seen the document before, and I assume there were reasons for asking those questions, maybe because those documents are not going to be introduced when the Defence tries to introduce them, I don't know. But here he hasn't seen the document, he's being asked to give an opinion. He's trying to give his opinion. Now, I don't know what Mr. Scott wants. Either he should limit the question -- but he can't be asking an opinion then cut the gentleman off in the middle of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't ask for an opinion. I think my question -- I'll be happy to restate it. I think my question was quite clear and it had nothing to do with price. The question was the allocation of phone lines, and my question specifically was:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it in fact the case that in the summer of 1992 and thereafter there was phone service, you mentioned yourself a few moments ago, 480 lines and at least some of these lines were allocated in fact as described by Mr. Stojic in the opening paragraph, the HVO military including the Main Staff and the Government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That's true, correct? And my question has nothing to do with price. They had telephone service?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have to express my disagreement. The document has to do with prices and charging for services. If you permit me, I will explain; and if you don't, well let us then just say that I disagree with your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. This document was copied to --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you permit me, I will explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the question of the witness is properly addressed to the Bench. It's for the Bench to give permission. I think a document's been put to the witness. He's seeking to explain it, and, Your Honours, I do think it may clarify matters if he's allowed a couple of minutes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, let me respond --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. I too am trying to understand both questions and answers. We have a document from Mr. Stojic who at the time was in charge of the defence department. Based on this, there could be a military dimension to this document. It includes six points. The first is to reduce the number of telephone connections linked up to the telephone central. Second item, it seems to have to do with expenses and charging for the service or for the telephone lines. Third item, which seems rather novel to me, the defence department seems to be the owner of all the telephone connections. So this document raises a series of questions not tackled specifically by the Prosecutor but in a general way, and I would like to know whether as of the date of this document there was some intervention by the defence department, maybe because of the wartime conditions, in order to control telephone lines or reduce their number and better control the expenses. Because this document seems to say that the defence department is the exclusive owner of all these telephone connections. You at the time, you were involved in this telephone system. As far as you know back then, did the defence department claim to be the owner of these 480 numbers - Because we know that number of 480 - and as an owner, did they exercise their right of control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence department did not have any connections that were under the management of the PTT HZ HB public company, but the defence department and the commanders and soldiers used the telephone services of the public company, and they were in the offices, in the apartments, and other places were subscribers to the public service for which the public service sent them bills. Director Zulj and we from the board insisted that these services be paid, that they be paid equally by individual civilians and soldiers and commanders all equally. They could either pay it themselves or the ministry could pay those bills for them. We needed money in order to renew the telecommunications system, and so the sense here is to limit the number of users, military personnel, and to limit the number of impulses that they could use. Because I know, I remember, that there was resistance, the soldiers wanted to get a free telephone service and we asked that the telephone services be paid for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, why is the defence department interested in the issue? Why is it interested in private telephone lines? Look at item 1, private lines are mentioned. So why is the defence department interested in this? Is it for reasons connected to defence or for other reasons? Why are they interested in this because this is an order? Can you answer this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Command to military personnel. This is how I am experiencing it. So military personnel had telephones in their private home, and that telephone was something that they were not paying for, in the belief that the Ministry of Defence should be the one to pay for this service. We asked from the Ministry of Defence to say who had the right to this free service and who did not, whose telephone bills they will pay and whose they will not. Those whose bills would not be paid by the Ministry of Defence needed to pay their bill themselves. So I see this letter as restriction of telephone service use for military personnel. This is how I understand it. Perhaps I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to make a statement of my personal legal view on the dispute that has arisen. I am of the firm opinion that when a party is questioning a witness, that party determines the questions and it's not for the witness to say what he would like to talk about. And when there's a document, normally there are several issues that could be raised, it is for the party that puts the question to determine which are to be discussed because otherwise that party loses control over the time. The Defence often - and understandably - complains about lack of time. I think if the Prosecution does so there's no reason to treat it in a different way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always enlightening and I am grateful for your personal opinion, and I would concur completely that it's for the party to decide the questions. But my intervention relates to the answer, and the witness -- the overriding objection -- responsibility, as you know, is to ensure a fair trial. This document, of course, is important to the Prosecutor, which is why my learned friend put it to the witness. The only reason why I rose is that I did think, and I think the questions by the Presiding Judge, were very helpful to cast a light on this document which is put forward by the Prosecution. Of course the aim is to get to the truth, and I think the additional questions have served a very useful purpose. But, Your Honour, I agree with the underlying premise of Your Honour's underlying view of the control of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott. The witness has told us that this document has to do with military telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour. I do appreciate the Chamber's questions and they were similar to the ones that I was about to get to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to hopefully shed further light on this, would you go, please, to 1D 00905, 1D 00905. Sir, this -- relating back to this issue and the same Mr. Zulj that we've been talking about this afternoon, this is a document entitled: "Empowerment" over the name President Mate Boban, issued from the main headquarters, Grude, 4 May 1992, empowering Mr. Zulj to carry out work on the necessary PTT connections in the territory, as Mr. Karnavas will say, I give emphasis to that, in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, with the purpose of defending of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And then we saw the document a few moments ago, sir, and we'll go back -- I told you we would go back to it again, if you could go to 1D 00906, 1D 00906, it should be the next one but if you don't have it we'll find it. Sir, this is the document we looked at a few moments ago, and I said we would come back to the content of it. This document dated the 20th of May, 1992, again by Mr. Zulj again raises the issue of the allocation of communication lines, and he talks about: "According to the wartime technical criteria of PTT communications, namely in the ratio of 1:5 (one channel = five subscribers). "Directors of PTT units shall arrange the disconnection according to this criterion through HVO command." Item 4: "Special commission on behalf of the main headquarters shall control the execution of this command." The military, sir, minister of -- ministry of defence, the department of defence, was controlling the telephone system during this time-period, correct? It was a matter of defence.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't read it the way you do, that's not my understanding, and I have to explain this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm sorry, time does not allow. It talks about the criterion, the wartime criterion. Wartime technical criterion of PTT connections 1:5, where did that criterion come from?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One telephone exchange, a thousand numbers has about a hundred connections. And at that time we never went to full capacity. In wartime conditions there is an increase in demand, more phone calls are placed, and in order to make sure that this traffic can be sustained, it was necessary to reduce the number of subscribers. Now we're talking about the telephone exchanges that were not destroyed, that were still operational. The number of subscribers had to be reduced in order to make sure that the other priority users could use telephones without any obstructions. It is quite clear that staff in some municipality - I'm talking about the HVO - could set those priorities. In cooperation between the PTT and the staffs, it was necessary to determine whose telephone lines could be disconnected, who no longer resided there, who no longer needed to have a telephone line, so that the telephone lines that were at the disposal could then be allocated to priority users, those who really had to have a phone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Priority users being the military and the government, correct, among others perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military, the government, the services, hospitals, utilities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you'll go, for example, to Exhibit 1D 00624, and we'll provide it to you, sir, if you can't find it. 1D 00624. Sorry, here's one. If we can look on e-court, please, if it assists. Sir, this is a -- I just want to point this out to you as an example. Here is a document in September of 1992 where a telephone line is being allocated to the University of Mostar. So is that an example of a priority user?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some reason -- well, this is an example of a non-priority user because at that time the university was not used to provide education; it was used by other services for the purposes of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go, please, to Exhibit 1D 02670, 1D 02670. We'll assist you, sir. Sir, this is a report that you discussed yesterday and you gave it a date -- when asked about this one yesterday, you gave it a date of the summer of 1992, and I want to move quickly, please. The end of the first long paragraph says the following, it's talking about: "Thanks to early" -- well, that whole long sentence. "Thanks to early preparations, the prompt action taken by experts," et cetera, et cetera, at the end of that long sentence, "... some lines for the most essential needs have been established and fairly successfully maintained," correct? That's a report that you wrote.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it here. It's -- I can't see this part that you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under the title: "Introduction," there is a long block of text and at the end of that particular block of text there is a talk about: "Thanks to early preparations, the prompt action taken by experts, the existence of the UNIS Telekom factory, Mostar, which makes telecommunication equipment and has experts for design and installation, the help from the Croatian Post and Telecommunications, Centre Split, and the Nikola Tesla factory in Zagreb," as a result of all of that, "some lines for the most essential needs have been established and fairly successfully maintained." Now, have you found it yet?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I think I have a different document.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please show it here up in the screen. Would you please show it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 02670. Just I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document but I can't find this text that you're reading. Sir, I just can't find this text that you're reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have the same problem, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then maybe my numbering is wrong, Your Honour, and I apologise if it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's the very first paragraph of the first page under "introduction" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you have to go down about six or seven lines -- seven, and it's sort of on the right hand: "Thanks to early preparations ...," that's the part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, have you found it, please?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's a report that you wrote, too; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I drafted this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Down under the heading that's titled: "UNIS Telekom," you describe that enterprise Mostar, and we're not going to again go through the whole thing, but you describe there the equipment made, and it's halfway down through the paragraph, sir. "The equipment made and installed by this enterprise can be found across the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and further afield, although the aggressor occupied the factory for several months, the enterprise maintained its production and services during the war because semi-finished equipment, some reproduction materials and parts and most of the manufacturing equipment, which could have been dismantled and relocated, had been relocated in time." So isn't it correct, sir, that throughout this time-period, 1992/1993, the Herceg-Bosna government, the HVO, had a substantial advantage in having this working telecommunications factory located in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They did have a great value in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, one specific question in terms of some of these relay stations that have been discussed. Do you recall when the relay station was established and operational at Cubren near Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cubren.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, if I'm pronouncing it wrong my apologies, but near Kiseljak, Cubren?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Cubren.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell me when that radio station -- excuse me, my apologies, the relay station was established and operational at that location?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, it was in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with Sarajevo and Mostar being -- your statement that they were cut off, I believe I heard you say several times yesterday that there were times -- there did come a time, in fact, that you were able - you, the Herceg-Bosna apparatus, the HVO - was able to establish telephone links or communication links with Central Bosnia. Do you recall when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, throughout that year we gradually dealt with the communication lines with the enclaves in Central Bosnia; some may have been done later, but most of the work was done in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So can we understand, sir, that at various times in 1993 communication links were established from Mostar to Central Bosnia by telephone?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I can say that this relay station at Cubren was also used for that purpose. Some communication was set up with Kiseljak through it, and later on it was possible to connect also towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which in fact was my next question. I think you've said several times that you got -- you - and again, I'm speaking collectively, the HVO - got very close to Sarajevo, to making a connection, I think you said you could see Sarajevo. When did that occur? When did you get so close -- when did this system get so close to Sarajevo that you could see Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that at this time it was the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, not the HVO. The PTT Herceg-Bosna public company did this work, and it dealt with the issues related to linking up all the places that were under the HVO control. And in this respect there were several --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- stages --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... able to see Sarajevo in connection with -- in making a telecommunications connection or a communication connection with it? My question asks for a date.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions by Judge Trechsel yesterday to -- again to be more clear about when this state of "non-communication" ended. And for counsel this dialogue appears at pages 21 and 22 of yesterday's transcript. And you said: "From that time on," you're referring to when it started in May of 1992, "from that time on we put in intensive efforts to set up various communications systems in the areas that we had access to, and in this manner we were able to set up communications not only within Herzegovina itself but using those points that we had access to we were able to establish links between Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, and likewise at a point from which you could see Sarajevo we've made it possible for Sarajevo to link up with this network; in other words, for Sarajevo to be linked up with Mostar." And Judge Trechsel says: "And at what time was that?" And you said: "I think in April of 1994." And Judge Trechsel's next question, and this is really where I was wanting to get to, Judge Trechsel's next question: "And did you do that via directional-beam aerials, did the dish antennas go point to point?" And you said: "Yes, yes, that's how we did it." So when was this directional -- these directional-beam aerials, when were those put in place?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment when communications were -- began to be set up between the PTT Herceg-Bosna public company and the PTT company headquartered in Sarajevo was when this meeting was held in Sarajevo. We said that the meeting was held between the 27th and the 29th of April, 1994. At that time, we asked all the PTT units and all the technical personnel in the PTT company to establish links with the other side wherever it was possible, and in some areas this was done quickly and in other areas it took a long time. As far as I know, there were no problems on our side. The same kind of communications had to be set up on the side of Mostar and that's what we did. So it was a process. And I think that we gradually improved both our relations and the communications themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that this might be the time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. It's 20 to 6.00. We'll now break for 20 minutes, so we resume at 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Staying on some questions that were raised by -- again by Judge Trechsel yesterday, but after moving on from the directional-beam aerial, Judge Trechsel also asked you about the possibility of short-wave or long-wave radio communication. And you got into a discussion, sir, of the differences between short-wave and long-wave and ultra short-wave, but I'm not sure we ever got a clear answer to Judge Trechsel's question. It's correct, is it not, that radio signals and radio communications between Sarajevo and Mostar were possible and in fact was going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that radio communications - in other words, Radio Sarajevo - could be received in Mostar if the medium-range transmitter working, at I think 612 kilohertz was operational, and it appears that it too was in an area where it was at risk from the Serb forces. I don't know that because I didn't really follow that. I know that we could receive this radio intermittently in Mostar during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And apart from radio in terms of commercial radio, and by that I mean perhaps news and music radio stations, there could also be radio communication between Sarajevo and Mostar in terms of voice and data communication by radio; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not possible. As far as the public telecommunications system is concerned, it was not possible. As for ham radio operators, they were able to communicate throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the world, but this was not telephone communication. It's a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So for example, those ham operators that were working at the Rondo, they were in radio communication with Sarajevo or anywhere else; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ham operators, when their equipment was working could communicate with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, satellite telephones --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one remark. I know that you're fed up with those problems. In our language ham radio operators are people who work their radio stations as amateurs. In English it is translated as ham operators. At this Tribunal I don't know whether the sense of amateur is preserved, ham operators, and this is lost here. From the answers that we got here, I'm not sure that the translation you received tells you that these are amateurs, not part of a structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I can assure you, if one -- I've looked it up on LEO and ham operator is translated into the equivalent of German of amateur radio operator. So it's exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I appreciate very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I remember that there were some problems with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hope I will not be understood as testifying or as taking over from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to be clear on that, though, whatever the status, professional or amateur, of the person, the human being, sitting at the machine, the technology existed and the technology established communications between Sarajevo and Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say once again that it depends on what kind of communication you want to have. As regards the public company, the postal communications that the PTT public company was providing, there was no communication. There was this commercial radio as you call it, which could be received intermittently in Mostar, and there were ham radio operators. As I said yesterday, there were some satellite communications too, but I don't know how that functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. Let's go back to ham radios. I assume that these ham radio operators had equipment to communicate between them, a ham operator in Mostar and surroundings can contact another ham operator in London, for example. And he would do this using short waves. So at this moment these ham operators, do they automatically have to go through the PTT relay stations or could you tell us whether their own system is totally independent from the PTT infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ham operators have a system that is independent from any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question. Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were about to say, sir, about satellite phones which was the next item I wanted to come back to. Mr. Karnavas certainly asked a number of questions about satellite phones and some phones that were apparently available to Mr. Izetbegovic or others. So that technology did exist at the time and apparently was used in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the 1992-1994 time-period; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This technology did exist at the time. If the documents that were presented yesterday are correct, then it was used in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are you suggesting, sir, that technology was only -- for some reason only available to the Muslims and not available to the Croats or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was available both to the HVO but somebody needed to sign a contract, obtain the equipment, and sign a usage contract, meaning that that -- that they would have to then pay for the services provided by the telephone company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed that anyone in the area of HZ HB obtained such telephones; perhaps they did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your testimony, sir, is you don't know; correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you said -- in one of your reports, and if you forgive me I'm not going to pull out every document that we looked at in the last two days, but I'll represent to you that in one of your reports you talked about the mobile telephone network. What was the status of mobile telephones in 1992/1993? I know they weren't as prevalent as they are today, but they were around and they were used, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our region, I'm talking about the Herceg-Bosna area, we didn't have the capacity for mobile telephones at that time. But the mobile phone network in Croatia, the so-called analog mobile telephones which are quite different from such phones today, did exist. There was a very high hill in Croatia, in Dalmatia, the hill is called Biokovo, where the device transmitting these signals was installed and that covered partially the Herzegovina area, and that is how it was possible to use these phones for the most essential purposes. These were analog system mobile telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could go on to some examples -- what I'm going to put to you at least as examples of some communications that were going on around this time, and I believe that probably for the balance of the evening hopefully it will be a bit simpler, these will all be P exhibits in the first binder, binder number 1. So if you can turn first of all to P 00237, P 00237. Sir, I'd appreciate very much your cooperation in moving through these documents as efficiently as we both can. I'm not so much interested in the content as the -- as opposed to what they indicate in terms of communication. So if you have P 00237, this is an order going out over the name Milivoj Petkovic on the 3rd of June, 1992, to Livno, Tomislavgrad, and Citluk. Item number 1: "Send an aggregate daily report as you have done up to now, in writing and by courier. "2. Immediately report all enemy actions and activities by telephone, giving the following information ..." Would you agree with me, sir, that apparently when Mr. Petkovic --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- or someone on his behalf signed this, he thought telephone service was available; correct? Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you will go, please, to Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, just one moment, please. You can see here Livno, Tomislavgrad, and Citluk. There was no destruction there and that's where the network or the communications were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps -- perhaps you can assist us, and if you can I'm sure everyone will be grateful.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you've come here then to talk about is then -- you're talking about the civilian communications that operated through -- directly through the PTT system, but you're not telling us -- you haven't told us anything about the communication facilities used by the military. Is that what you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object again, Your Honour. Perhaps -- perhaps there's a -- something is being lost in translation and I'll try to be as measured as I possibly can. The gentleman came here to testify about matters related to communications, PTT, whether civilian or military. He was shown a document. He indicated that for those reasons there was an ability to communicate. Perhaps -- perhaps it might be better, and we could save some time, if he was simply asked, where he was able -- in which areas you were able to communicate and in which areas you were not. And then if he wants to be impeached further, if he can, fine; otherwise, I believe the gentleman has indicated yesterday that at times there was a -- they were able to communicate within certain locations. He has never testified otherwise. The question I would imagine now for the Prosecution that might be interesting is where. I think that's the real issue. There's no real contention, and I don't think there's a need to take somewhat of a confrontational tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, perhaps the courtroom will be shocked for me to say that I fully agree with Mr. Karnavas on this occasion, and that's really what I intended to go, the direction I intended to go in, but that's not the way my question came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So let me restate it, sir. What I meant to say, and I admit I didn't put it well, perhaps you can assist us rather than going through a large number of documents, can you confirm to the Judges, sir, that throughout large parts of Herzegovina, including Livno and Tomislavgrad and Citluk and Stolac and Capljina and Siroki Brijeg, for examples, there was telephone service available, at least to the military and the government, throughout -- from mid-1992 to the end of 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the Mostar telecommunications centre in Mostar was shelled in May 1992, and all the installations under the control of the HVO were functioning very well but the communications -- external communications -- actually, internal connections between different places functioned very well, but the communications with the outside world, abroad, were functioning with difficulties because we had a reduced number of communications towards Croatia, i.e., the world. At this moment when this is being written, the communications were quite good. When the shelling began, very quickly the free territories in Herzegovina, the free territories which were under the control of the HVO, very quickly had reduced communications, proceeding with difficulty, and they had to be satisfied to give precedence to priority users, but the communications did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... correction. On page 76, line 13, the gentleman indicated that up until the shelling of May 1992 all the installations that were under the control of the HVO were functioning. So that was my understanding from my colleague, and then -- the rest of the answer is fine. He's repeated this on earlier occasions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question was -- to you was -- again, I think everyone in the courtroom, we're trying to see if we can make some -- move efficiently. And the question -- my question to you was not what happened before the shelling of the PTT building in Mostar in May 1992. I think we've all heard about that about 15 or 20 different times, but after that, from mid-1992 to the end of 1993 into 1994, in the Herzegovina region - and I named a number of locations - perhaps what you can call internal communications, throughout that time-period, subject to some disruptions from time to time, can the Judges understand that there was telephone communication, at least among the so-called priority users?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And based on that we'll cut out about eight or nine or ten exhibits. Would you please go next to, just as one example, P 07541. If you have that, sir, this is a list of prisoners of war dated the 10th of January, 1994, and out of the ones that I just literally flipped through to try to cut down the number of exhibits, if you look at the top of the B/C/S original, Serbo-Croatian original, of that document, would you agree with me, sir, that the top of that document appears to have what we call a fax information, a line of fax information, indicating that it was faxed and it went apparently to the 058-521-771? Do you have it, sir? That's P 07541. Do you have it? Do you see the line on top, sir?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that is what most of us consider to be an indication that a document has been faxed?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, would you look, please, next at Exhibit P 01572, P 01572.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that this is in fact a telephone directory of the HVO Main Staff for March 1993, essentially a telephone book for the HVO Main Staff and various HVO units throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, but I haven't found the Croatian version yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should be behind --

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for an example, on the first page under department of defence HZ HB you see the name for Mr. Bruno Stojic, and you see I think three telephone numbers associated with his name. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We won't go through it. There's no point in going through others I think. Would you look at Exhibit P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- I have not found a date for this document and I would be interested to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. On the top of the front page -- at the bottom of the front page I think you will find the date March 1993, the cover of the directory, if you will, do you have it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could go next of all -- as just another example to P 03053, P 03053.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you see again, this is a document that was put out sometime in 1993. I'm afraid that we just have a blank 1993, once again a list of telephone numbers for various HVO units.

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you could next go, please, to P 01818. Now, sir, I realize you may or may not have seen this document before today, but given what the international observers and different organizations were trying to do in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1992 and 1993, 1994, would it surprise you that as part of their work they would prepare a list of telephone numbers to use in carrying out their work? And if I can direct your -- there is a second heading, number 2, Government of Herceg-Bosna HVO, and you'll see a number of individuals, officials, President Mate Boban, general secretary; president of HV government, Jadranko Prlic; a number of telephone numbers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, if I told you that in fact one of the witnesses who came and testified here still had some of these same telephone numbers on his cell phone when he came to the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could next go, please, to P 02172 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The witness said something which the interpreters had not heard. Witness, could you please repeat your last answer what you have said; the interpreters did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor said that one of the witnesses today still has these numbers in their mobile telephone, and I said he probably did not update his mobile telephone directory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You could be right. If we could go to P 02172. Turning a bit from telephone, if I can just ask you, you have that, sir. This is a document that seems to indicate the existence and operation of a telephone network in giving a set of numbers, ID numbers, stations, the persons or units with that radio location or call-sign, and a code or call-sign for each of the people. The first one is for May 1993. The second page is for June 1993. The third page is for July 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you possibly just have a moment -- well, I won't say it. Number 1 for May 30, the code-name for the chief of the HVO Main Staff was Atila in May 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you go, please, to P 03866. If you have that, sir -- now, this talks about the organization of packet radio communications. In the course of your work with communications in this time-period, 1992/1993/1994, did you ever hear of or become familiar with a form of radio communication called packet communication?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that that's something like -- a bit like a field fax, a text -- typed text is entered in, it is sent by a radio signal, and then you get a text print-out at the other end?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a radio network for data transfer. You can receive a fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that, sir. We have been able to move more quickly. I do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the last document, Witness, which is a military-type document, this type of communication, packet radio communication, I see telephone numbers and I see always that they start with 058. In other documents that we saw before, these three figures were the same for basically all the numbers. This would seem to indicate that at least in August 1993 telephones were working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was shown these documents, but I did not get a question so I don't know why they were shown to me. First of all, I can speak in some detail about communications that were part of the public telecommunications system because that's what I worked on, that's what I knew about. Of course there were military communications systems that were used by military units. They used radio equipment to communicate, including packet radio and voice transmission network. Of course those communications existed and they were used. I think that the question here is -- well, I did not contest the fact that some places in Herzegovina had communications at all times. Sometimes they were better, sometimes they were worse. Mostar itself was cut off for one or two days, but some minimum level of communications was re-established quite soon. Now, the question is where the 058 appears. At that time, because we were unable to solve it in any other way, we had some direct connections to the Split exchange and priority users availed themselves of that. That is so-called remote user, a subscriber, a subscriber that is connected let's say from Citluk to Split, but that's not unusual at all. So I couldn't really speak in any detail about military communications. You need to call a witness who deals with those issues because this is not something that I've ever dealt with in my life. But as far as the civilian, public, telecommunications system, I consider myself an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the document under item 4, it is in your language at the top of page 3. In group 4 we can see that there is HVO Mostar, GSS Mostar, and then under number 6 I can see that it is the office of the president of HZ HB, and there is 088/662-760, that's the number. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me what document because several documents were mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, it is 3866.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go to page 3 in your language, top of the page. You can see "grupa," look under 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that there is a number, 088/662-760.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, before the war every larger town had its area code. Mostar's code was 088, Split was 058, Livno was 080, Central Bosnia was 071, and so on. And during the war the area codes remained the same. It was changed later. Now we have a different area code for those areas, but this was -- these were the area codes that were in use before the war and remained to be used during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the date when this document was made, on the 1st of August, 1993, with regard to the office of the president, did it have a telephone line? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, for sure it did, August 1993. At that time our communications were pretty much regular. It was in August 1992 that the communications were quite bad, but by August 1993 they were already up to the very good level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And while we're on that document, sir, before you move on and perhaps I was a bit too hasty. But on P 03866, in addition to the number that the President has focused on, would you please also look at in group number 1 -- the first one starts with HVO Main Staff, number 1, but as you continue down the list do you see number 6, Central Bosnia operative zone Vitez; number 7, Bosnian Posavina; number 8 Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade, Kiseljak; number 10, Novi Travnik; number 11, Zepce; number 12, Vares; 13 Busovaca; 14, Vitez again; and 15, Sarajevo. Do you see the packet communication links listed for all of those locations?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are with this document, Witness, in the English text on the bottom of page 3, and in the B/C/S text I think it's on page 3, the first paragraph after the list of six numbers. There is reference also to short-wave radio, KV short wave set. Would that be something like ham radio, technically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's different. I think it's different. To be quite frank, I'm not all that familiar with this type of equipment because I have never dealt with military communications. Ham operators have transmitters and radio stations that can transmit over a huge area, and that is their purpose, to transmit over the whole world. And there is a special period of day when the signal can be transmitted very clearly and very far, and that's when they work. I would say that these are short-distance radios that cover a very broad area around the repeater, in particular because they have encryption equipment so that they cannot be intercepted, and everybody can intercept conversations over ham radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But they also use short wave, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean ham radio operators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, short wave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a correction, on page 83, line -- page 84, line 21, he didn't say "broad area" but short area, small area, something to the -- but it was the opposite of broad. Short-distance radios that cover a very short area, that's how my colleague heard it, but we can ask for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you clarify that, Witness, what did you say? A short-distance and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're talking about military radio equipment, there are different kinds. Usually they cover a very narrow area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- a short distance. Radio ham operators, they cover broad areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few more seconds on this. Please look at page 4 in this document, right at the bottom of the document, you can see a stamp with some indications, various indications, regarding the stamp. You keep in mind that you had the HVO GS, telegram 5320, 31st of August, 1993, and then the time is indicated, and you can see some acronyms, TLP, TGR, TLF, RRV, ZV, and RV. So TLF, I suppose, stands for telephones; TGR, telegraphs; TLP, that stands for teleprinter; RV, I suppose that's radio communications. The documents of the 1st of August, 1993, that was sent to all operational areas looks as though it was sent by radio communication because you have RV that is underlined. The very fact that there is a stamp in which telephone, TLF, is indicated, does it show that back then there were various telecommunication systems available to the entities sending messages. Here this time it came from the Main Staff and it was sent to the operational areas, but it was sent by a packet radio. I'm interested in the fact that a TLF is mentioned in the stamp, which may indicate that in August 1993 telephones were working too. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is your task to send a document, you can send it in a number of ways. It depends on the level of confidentiality. The military will probably use the type of communications that allows encryption, and as far as I know packet radio does make it possible. Of course there are other types of communications, but it doesn't mean that they existed all over the place. The military probably provided radio communications and packet radio communications wherever it was operating, where its units were operating. It couldn't send a unit out unless that unit had communications equipment that worked. I keep telling you that I'm an expert in public communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Witness, it occurs to me when looking at the stamp that the second T in PTT traditionally means telegraph, and it is one means of communication we have not touched upon at all yet. Normally it would have been within your realm and competencies. Can you tell us anything about communication by telegraph, particularly 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only thing I can tell you is that at times it was a widely used network, the telegraph network in public communications. But when Telefax appeared, this type of communication was set aside and in recent times telephone lines were used for telegraph communications but by those who needed it. To my knowledge, those are financial institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, I have simply misspoken. I wanted to ask about telegram because that is mentioned here. This is apparently a telegram and it's nowadays it doesn't exist anymore I think, but at that time it was still one possibility and what was the situation for that in Mostar in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Telegrams are a different thing. Telegrams are received by post offices. Post offices received letters and telegrams, and then they deliver it in any way they can, by telephone or by fax or by teleprinter. But military organizations probably used this type of service more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But was it possible in a different way than what we have already spoken about, you do not have to repeat all that, to communicate by telegram between Mostar and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to understand that telegrams are transmitted over telephone lines. So if you don't have telephone lines, then this kind of communication is impossible. There is not a separate network for the transmission of telegrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, if we could move forward in the last few minutes here and see if we can again make some progress. I would like you to turn your attention to - and this is a separate binder - the entire binder was marked as Exhibit 10633, 10633, it's titled for the record and for the usher: "Examples of communications with Central Bosnia including Sarajevo." And I do have -- you will see -- look at the schedule, sir, and I had the impression that you at least read English based on various things that you've said, but I also -- if you look behind -- I think at least as to the last column, the column on the right, the far right, you'll find a Serbo-Croatian version in your binder I hope. And, sir, what I've done here, we can go -- well, if we had enough time we could go through all 48, I suppose, I think it's 48 -- I'm sorry, 46. Various communications that these documents seem to indicate on the dates indicated are between Sarajevo and other places outside of Sarajevo, including large -- in instances Mostar and Grude or in some places in Herzegovina. Perhaps just to give you some examples so everyone in the courtroom knows the process involved here. In the binder there's a separate set of tab numbers, and if you can go, please, to P 00346, P 00346. It should be the third document in the binder. You will see I think, sir, if you have that, this is a letter dated the 26th of July, 1992, from Mr. Markesic secretary general of the HDZ BH, and says: "Reference: Your letter number U 46/92 of 22nd July 1992." And again, sir, my purpose of showing you these documents is not to discuss the content of the document, but doesn't that document indicate it is in response to a document coming from a response -- it's going to the constitutional court, excuse me, indicating that a letter had been received to which this letter is responding between the 22nd of July and the 26th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ILIJA KOZULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please look at the very next document, I'll to keep it as simple as possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for point of clarification, we should understand that this is within Sarajevo, so it's Sarajevo to Sarajevo as I understand it. So -- and that's the whole point --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- that's the whole point, and I'm going to be hitting hard at this issue at some point that when they claim notice they give notice to HDZ Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is the constitutional court. If they were really interested, they would be directing it someplace else. So if we're going to use this as an example, it's a poor example, bad one, choose another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, it may be a bad example; if it was, my apology, and there is no reason to get too worked up about it. If I'm mistaken, if we selected -- my apologies to both the witness and the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
